newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan jobless rate eases, no big improvement seen.
newsitem.headline: Japan jobless rate eases, no big improvement seen.

text.p: Japan's unemployment rate edged down last month but the job situation is not expected to improve dramatically in the near future, given slow economic recovery, the government said Friday.
The nation's unemployment rate fell to 3.3 percent in November from 3.4 percent in October, a shade below the record 3.5 percent seen in the summer, official data showed.

While Japan does not have the double-digit jobless rates of some Western countries, the climb in the rate above 3 percent since early 1995 has caused concern in a nation which has had minimal unemployment for most of the postwar era.
By comparison, the jobless rate in France is now about 12 percent, while the rates are about 10 percent in Germany, 7 percent in Britain and 5 percent in the United States.
"It is difficult to predict that Japan's jobless rate will improve dramatically in the near future," a senior government official told reporters.
Last week, the government said it expected the unemployment rate to average 3.3 percent in the fiscal year starting on April 1, compared with its estimate of 3.4 percent for 1996/97.

Japan's economy has been struggling to recover from a slump that set in after the collapse of the 1980s economic "bubble" of inflated asset prices, forcing companies to cut costs and restructure their operations to maintain profits.
Economists said Japanese companies are likely to continue streamlining their business into the next fiscal year.
Many economists predict that the economic recovery will slow in early 1997, especially after a planned rise in the sales tax in April to 5 percent from 3 percent.
"November data showed that the employment situation remains severe...but there are some bright aspects in the data," the government official said.

The slight drop in the jobless rate in November was due mainly to a dip in the number of people who voluntarily left their jobs in November. "Some of those people may have found a job," the official said.
The number of employed people in November rose 0.9 percent from a year earlier to 64.97 million, increasing for a ninth straight month.
Unemployment among middle-aged or older workers, who have been targeted for streamlining, fell in November after several months of continuous rises.
Another closely watched employment figure, the jobs-to-applicants ratio, rose to 0.74 in November from 0.73 in October. This means there were 74 job offers for every 100 applicants.
Economists said the employment situation is unlikely to worsen as private consumption and capital spending are expected to help sustain the economic recovery.

The recovery is also supported by stable prices. The government released data on Friday showing that nationwide consumer prices in November rose 0.5 percent year-on-year, but fell 0.3 percent month-on-month.
